stem: A 17-year-old boy comes to the office with right knee pain after being tackled in rugby the previous day.  He has difficulty bearing weight, and it feels as if his knee is unstable.  On examination, a large effusion is present, and the patient has limited range of motion due to pain.  X-ray of the right knee demonstrates an avulsion fracture of the tibial spine, as shown in the exhibit.  Injury to which of the following structures is most likely present in this patient?​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​​​​​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​
explanation:
This patient has an avulsion fracture of the tibial spine, a bony eminence located on the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia, and the distal insertion site of the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL).

An avulsion fracture occurs when a fragment is pulled away from the main part of the bone by attached soft tissue (eg, ligament, tendon), often due to an abrupt tensile force being applied (eg, sudden change in direction, twisting during a tackle).  In adolescents and children, avulsion fractures may occur because of the relative weakness of the incompletely ossified bone (eg, tibial spine) compared with soft tissue attachments (eg, ACL).

Avulsion fracture of the tibial spine frequently indicates disruption of the ACL (ie, ACL detachment with the fracture fragment).  The mechanism of injury is usually the same as that of ACL tears: an excessive, often twisting force causing valgus stress on the knee and/or anterior translation of the tibia on the femur.  Clinical features include sudden pain and a large effusion due to hemarthrosis.  Patients may be unable to bear weight and have limited range of motion.  Because the ACL functions to resist the motion of anterior tibial translation and internal tibial rotation, a feeling of instability following the injury may be described.

(Choice B)  The posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) attaches proximally to the medial femoral epicondyle and distally to the posterior intercondylar area of the tibia.  PCL avulsion fractures are rarer than ACL avulsion fractures and appear as a focal discontinuity on the posterior aspect of the tibia; they are best visualized on lateral x-ray.

(Choices C and D)  The medial collateral ligament (MCL) attaches proximally to the medial epicondyle of the femur and distally to the proximal tibia.  The lateral collateral ligament (LCL) attaches to the lateral femoral epicondyle and distally to the fibular head.  Avulsion fractures associated with these ligaments are extraarticular (vs intraarticular) and are located at the medial femur or tibia (eg, MCL) or lateral femur or fibular head (eg, LCL) instead of the anterior midline.

(Choice E)  The patellar tendon attaches to the inferior pole of the patella proximally and the tibial tuberosity distally.  Patellar tendon avulsion fracture typically occurs at the attachment on the inferior pole of the patella; upward displacement of the patella may then occur due to unopposed pull of the quadriceps tendon.

(Choice F)  The medial patellofemoral ligament (PFL) and lateral PFL attach on the medial and lateral patella and the medial or lateral femoral epicondyles, respectively.  They function to stabilize the patella.  Injury most commonly occurs to the medial PFL when the patella dislocates laterally; associated avulsion fracture sometimes occurs at the medial patella.

Educational objective:The tibial spine is located in the anterior intercondylar region of the tibia and contains the distal attachment site of the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL).  Avulsion fractures of the tibial spine are usually associated with disruption of the ACL.​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​​​​​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​
